2026-10-27.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Home Building Finance Ireland will stop lending to small developers.
Small builders will no longer need planning permission to build homes.
The Government plans a law letting a State-backed lender fund land purchases before planning permission, to help small builders and speed up housing supply.
Cabinet has already approved and published new rules on building loans.
2026-10-27.exp: The passage says the Government intends legislation "aimed at alleviating the financial constraints that impede smaller homebuilders" so the lender could fund "land zoned for residential use prior to the granting of planning permission". Planning permission is still needed (B), lending is expanded, not stopped (A), and the plan has not yet gone to Cabinet (D).

2026-10-27.q: What can be inferred about small builders under the current rules?
opts: They may find it hard to start projects because they must pay the early costs largely from their own money.
They usually receive more funding than large developers.
Most of them already have planning permission before buying land.
They are not allowed to borrow from any lender.
2026-10-27.exp: Finance is "contingent upon the developer having already acquired a site and obtained planning permission", so "a substantial proportion of the initial costs must be met from the builder's own capital". Nothing says they get more funding (B), that they buy land with permission already (C), or that all borrowing is banned (D).

2026-10-27.q: Why does the writer mention that over 90 per cent of homebuilders complete fewer than 50 homes a year?
opts: To criticise small firms for building too slowly.
To argue that large developers should get the new loans instead.
To explain why the lender refuses most loan applications.
To show that small firms make up a large part of the sector, so the reform could have a wide effect.
2026-10-27.exp: The figure is given to show "the significance of the reform": "Small-scale firms therefore constitute a considerable share of the sector." The writer does not criticise them (A), favour large developers (B) or discuss refusals (C).

2026-10-27-2.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Bus and rail fares will be cut by 15 per cent in January.
Fares will rise by 15 per cent in January and will now be reviewed every year, a change pushed largely by the Department of Public Expenditure.
The National Transport Authority wants fares frozen until 2030.
The Minister for Transport has cancelled 140 bus and rail services.
2026-10-27-2.exp: The passage reports "a 15 per cent increase that will come into effect in January" and that fares "are to be subject to annual review", with the increase "largely attributable to considerable pressure from the Department of Public Expenditure". It is a rise, not a cut (A); the NTA backs reviews (C); and 140 services are being added, not cancelled (D).

2026-10-27-2.q: What can be inferred about the officials who complained in April?
opts: They wanted the 2022 fare cut made permanent.
They were opposed to any new public transport services.
They wanted the 2022 fare reduction reversed sooner than it was.
They worked for the National Transport Authority.
2026-10-27-2.exp: Officials "expressed dissatisfaction that the reversal had been delayed", so they wanted the cut undone earlier. They wanted fare revenue to "finance additional services", not to stop services (B), and the passage links the pressure to the Department of Public Expenditure, not the NTA (D).

2026-10-27-2.q: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
opts: To present a benefit the minister highlights alongside the fare increases.
To show that the minister has rejected the annual reviews.
To explain how the €940 million subsidy will be spent.
To report that fares will fall again next year.
2026-10-27-2.exp: Beginning with "Nevertheless", the paragraph balances the bad news with the minister's point that "approximately 140 new and improved services will be introduced next year". It does not say he rejects the reviews (B), detail the subsidy (C) or promise lower fares (D).

2026-10-27-3.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Ireland has met its 2030 nature targets ahead of schedule.
COP17 has agreed a new global target to replace the 2022 commitment.
Irish environmental groups praise the EU's new habitat laws.
At COP17 Ireland called for stronger action on biodiversity while admitting it is not on track to meet its own 2030 targets.
2026-10-27-3.exp: Ireland "advocated more substantial efforts to protect biodiversity at COP17", yet the minister "acknowledged that the country is 'not on track' to achieve its 2030 targets". It has not met them (A), no new target is reported (B), and the groups are critical of the EU (C).

2026-10-27-3.q: What can be inferred about the nature restoration fund mentioned by the minister?
opts: It has already paid for the restoration of most protected habitats.
It is still a plan rather than money that is currently available.
It is being paid for by the World Wildlife Fund.
It will replace all EU environmental funding in Ireland.
2026-10-27-3.exp: Ireland "has not yet allocated national funding" and the fund "is being developed", so it does not yet exist as available money. Habitats are still "in poor condition" (A), and nothing links it to the WWF (C) or to replacing EU funds (D).

2026-10-27-3.q: Which best describes the writer's tone in the passage?
opts: Celebratory, focusing on Ireland's success at the conference.
Indifferent, listing facts without any sense of their importance.
Concerned, presenting evidence that progress on protecting nature is falling short.
Angry, accusing the minister of lying about the targets.
2026-10-27-3.exp: The writer calls the evidence "far from encouraging" and Ireland's record "similarly concerning", citing a 73 per cent decline in wildlife and 90 per cent of habitats "in poor condition". There is no celebration (A), the importance is stressed (B), and the minister is reported as admitting the problem, not accused of lying (D).

2026-10-27-4.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Glenstal Abbey School will close in August 2028 because of falling demand for boarding and high running costs, with a gradual wind-down.
Glenstal Abbey School will close immediately and all students must leave this term.
Glenstal Abbey School is raising its fees to stay open.
The monastic community has decided to take over running the school.
2026-10-27-4.exp: The school "is scheduled to close in August 2028" and will "gradually cease operations"; the trustees cite "declining demand for boarding education and the considerable expense of operating a small boarding institution". The closure is not immediate (B), no fee rise is mentioned (C), and the monks call it "an exceptionally difficult decision" rather than taking over (D).

2026-10-27-4.q: What can be inferred about students who are not currently in second or fifth year?
opts: They will be able to stay at Glenstal until 2030.
They will receive a full refund of all past fees.
They will sit their Leaving Certificate early.
Many of them are likely to need to finish their schooling at another school.
2026-10-27-4.exp: Tuition continues normally "until June 2027; thereafter, students currently in second and fifth year will be permitted to complete their Junior and Senior Cycle". Since only these groups are allowed to finish, others will probably have to move. The school closes in 2028, not 2030 (A), and refunds (B) or early exams (C) are not mentioned.

2026-10-27-4.q: Why does the writer mention that similar pressures affect boarding schools in Ireland and abroad?
opts: To suggest other schools have treated Glenstal unfairly.
To indicate that the closure reflects a wider trend rather than a problem unique to Glenstal.
To encourage parents to choose schools outside Ireland.
To show that Glenstal's fees are lower than those abroad.
2026-10-27-4.exp: The trustees "noted that comparable pressures are affecting boarding schools both in Ireland and internationally", placing the decision in a broader context of "declining demand for boarding education". There is no claim of unfair treatment (A), advice to parents (C) or fee comparison (D).
